name: Romanesque
lede: Romanesque is a very dark, slightly reddish purple named in a 1920s color dictionary, a name it shares with the round-arched church style of about 950 to 1150, though no source we hold says why.

sections.title: A name with no recorded reason
sections.body:
Romanesque first appears as a color name in Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color*, which our library dates to 1926 for this entry, plate 46, L 10 [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS system files it as a dark purple, and the closest familiar name is [[aubergine]], about 10 units away [1]. Its lightness is only 22 on a scale of 100 and its chroma a low 19, so on screen it reads as a near-black plum [1].

Who chose the name, and whether it points to the architecture, is undocumented. None of our books ties this purple to a painted wall or to a pigment of the period. Treat the name as a label that the dictionary gave it, and the history below as the context a reader might expect, not as an origin.

sections.title: The period and its colors
sections.body:
Pastoureau dates the Romanesque period to about 950 to 1150 [3]. Churches of the time were not plain stone. He writes that after the year 1000 most founding prelates were chromophiles who held that color was a form of light, with a few exceptions such as Saint Bernard, the Cistercian who distrusted color [2][3]. Abbot Suger, who rebuilt Saint-Denis around 1130 to 1140, is the best-known example: he believed nothing was too beautiful to honor God [2]. A bitter quarrel between Cluniac and Cistercian monks over color in the church belongs to the same age [3].

Blue moved most. Before the twelfth century it was rare and unsettling in religious art [3]. Blue devils and demons make their first appearance in art of this age [3], and Pastoureau explains that blue was often seen as a semi-black, used for hell and its demons [2]. The painted wooden ceiling of St Martin at Zillis in Switzerland has a dark blue, almost black devil [2][3]. The books disagree on its date: Pastoureau's *Black* gives about 1120, while the caption in his *Blue* says about 1140, with a question mark [2][3].

The devil's palette in general was dark. Black and red dominated, and Satan was usually the most saturated, densest figure in the image [2]. Gage notes that blue glass in the Crucifixion window at Poitiers, from about 1180, stands in for the black of Christ's hair and beard [9]. Mary's colors moved the other way: in the Romanesque period her dress lightened and her cloak often became red, before blue took over in the early Gothic [4]. A limewood Virgin of about the year 1000, now in Liège, was first painted black, repainted blue in the thirteenth century, and refashioned again at the end of the seventeenth [3].

sections.title: Pigments that changed
sections.body: A wall of that age does not look as it was painted. The blue mineral aerinite has been reported in twelfth-century frescoes in Catalonia and Andorra [5]. Howard identified blue vivianite on a Romanesque wall painting that had altered to yellow, so the surface now reads as green overall [7]. In thirteenth-century Romanesque frescoes, atacamite is present as an alteration product of artificial azurite [6]. Color on an old wall has often shifted since it was laid down.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
As a painted color this dark purple is uncommon. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near the swatch appears in 39, or 0.16 per cent, and in 22 by the stricter within-painting test [10]. That is rarer than 60 per cent of the colors we have names for [10]. It peaks in the 1500s, in 7 of 2,231 paintings, which is 2.5 times the rate expected from the same museums [10]. Inside a painting it most often plays a shadow, in 45 per cent of the 22 [10].

The earliest dated match is [[painting:commons-Q3910903|a painting]] of 1342 by Ambrogio Lorenzetti, among 29 dated paintings with the color covering at least 2 per cent of the canvas, the latest from 1928 [10]. That is nearly two centuries after the Romanesque period ended, but the archive is thin before 1400, so this is a floor and not a first [10]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [10].

questions.q: What do our sources say about why this purple is called Romanesque?
choices: It was copied from a twelfth-century fresco
It was named after the pigment aerinite

questions.q: Which colors dominated the devil in Romanesque art, according to Pastoureau?
Why can a Romanesque wall painting look different today from when it was painted?
choices: Some pigments have altered, such as blue vivianite turning yellow so the surface looks green
